passage:
'Say buenos días to Don Rafael,' Mamá whispers on the stairs of their building in Guadalajara. Alejandro, five, shouts, 'Buenos días, Don Rafael!' as proudly as he says 'dinosaur'. The old man tips his hat and chuckles. Upstairs, Alejandro practises on his teddy: 'Don Teddy. Doña Teddy.'
That evening Mamá's friend Lupe visits, and he greets her with 'Don Lupe!' Everyone giggles.
'Tía Lupe,' Mamá corrects gently. 'Tía is for people we love like family.'
Alejandro thinks about it, then climbs into Lupe's lap. 'Tía Lupe,' he tries again, softer this time.

qa.q: What did Alejandro call Lupe at first?
qa.a: 'Don Lupe!'

qa.q: What was Alejandro feeling when he said 'Tía Lupe' softly and climbed into her lap?
qa.a: He felt warm and affectionate, starting to sense that 'tía' means someone loved like family, not just a fun sound.

qa.q: What did Mamá's correction get right?
qa.a: She corrected gently, without shaming him, and explained what 'tía' means, so Alejandro could link the word to warmth.

qa.q: How might Don Rafael feel when Alejandro greets him so loudly on the stairs?
qa.a: Don Rafael seems amused and pleased; being greeted with a respectful title by a small child makes him feel noticed.

grounding: Illustrates a young child who is taught respectful titles for older people, copies the sounds first, and only later begins to feel the warmth they carry.

passage:
In his first week at school, four-year-old Chetan shouts, 'Mehak! Mehak!' at the Class 5 girl who helps the little ones onto the bus. Sunita Ma'am crouches beside him. 'She's older than you. Say Mehak Didi.'
'Mehak Didi!'
He likes the sound so much that he says 'Didi' to the cook, the principal and the watchman. The watchman laughs. 'Bhaiya for me, little one.'
By Friday, when Chetan slips on the bus steps, Mehak Didi catches his hand and pulls him up. He holds her arm the whole ride home, saying 'Didi' quietly now, as if it means something.

qa.q: Who told Chetan to say 'Mehak Didi'?
qa.a: Sunita Ma'am.

qa.q: What does Chetan saying 'Didi' quietly on the ride home suggest he feels?
qa.a: It suggests he feels safe and fond of Mehak after she caught his hand, so the word now carries warmth, not just a fun sound.

qa.q: How could Sunita Ma'am help Chetan learn which titles fit which people?
qa.a: Explain gently, with a smile, who is Didi, Bhaiya or Aunty, and praise him when he gets it right instead of laughing at mix-ups.

qa.q: How might Mehak feel being called Didi by the new little boy?
qa.a: Mehak may feel proud and a bit responsible, since the title marks her as someone the younger children can lean on.

grounding: Shows a young child taught to use titles like didi and bhaiya for older people, who first copies the sound and later starts to feel the warmth in it.

passage:
"Trisha! Trisha, look!" Sahil waved his paper boat.
"Trisha didi, beta," said Mumma. "She's older than you."
"Trisha didi, look!"
Trisha laughed and knelt by the bucket. "Nice boat, Sahil."
Ten minutes later the milkman rang the bell. Sahil ran to the door. "Didi, milk!"
"That's Bhaiya, silly," Trisha giggled. "Didi is for girls."
"Bhaiya, milk!" Sahil beamed. The milkman grinned and ruffled his hair.
At night, when Trisha packed her bag to go home, Sahil hugged her leg. "Trisha didi, stay. You're my didi."
Trisha looked at Mumma. Mumma's eyes had gone soft.

qa.q: What did Sahil first call the milkman?
qa.a: Sahil called the milkman "Didi".

qa.q: What does Sahil's 'You're my didi' at bedtime suggest he feels?
qa.a: It suggests a warm, fond attachment to Trisha; the word is starting to mean closeness, not just a sound he copies.

qa.q: How could Mumma help Sahil learn titles gently?
qa.a: Keep modelling the right word calmly, as she did, and laugh along at mistakes like 'Didi, milk!' so he keeps trying.

qa.q: How might Trisha feel when Sahil hugs her leg?
qa.a: Trisha likely feels touched and fond, hearing the title said with real love.

grounding: Shows a young child copying titles like didi and bhaiya, first as sounds and then with warmth.

passage:
Observation note, Sunflower class, Tuesday

Trisha (5) has added "ji" to everything since her grandmother's visit. This morning: "Good morning, Aunty ji," to our cleaning helper, who smiled all day. Then "Water ji, please," and "Crayon ji." Soon the whole room was full of ji.

At snack time I asked her what "ji" means. She thought hard. "It's a nice word. For big people. So they feel happy."

What I did next: I showed the group a family photo chart, and we practised Dadi ji, Nana ji, Uncle, Aunty and Didi.

Sarita, class teacher

qa.q: What did Trisha say to the cleaning helper?
qa.a: Trisha said, "Good morning, Aunty ji."

qa.q: What does Trisha's answer about 'ji' suggest she is starting to feel?
qa.a: She seems pleased and caring; to her ji is a nice word that makes big people happy, so it already carries warmth.

qa.q: What did the teacher's next step add?
qa.a: The photo chart and practice with Dadi ji, Nana ji, Uncle, Aunty and Didi helped the children match titles to the right people.

qa.q: How might the cleaning helper feel after being called 'Aunty ji'?
qa.a: The helper felt respected and warmly noticed, which is why she smiled all day.

grounding: Shows a child copying an honorific everywhere at first and beginning to sense that it carries warmth for older people.

passage:
At Ajji's farm near Hassan, Ira, five, followed Chaitanya everywhere: to the cowshed, to the coconut heap, to the well.

"Chaitanya! Carry me!"

"Chaitanya anna," Ajji corrected from the doorway. "He's grown up."

"Chaitanya anna," Ira sang, like a new rhyme, then "Anna anna anna" until everyone laughed.

For days she said it only when Ajji was watching.

Then one evening she slipped on the wet steps near the well. Chaitanya reached her before she could cry, lifting her and brushing mud off her knee.

"Anna," Ira whispered into his shirt, and this time nobody had told her to.

qa.q: Where did Ira slip?
qa.a: Ira slipped on the wet steps near the well.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling when she whispered 'Anna' into his shirt?
qa.a: Ira felt safe and grateful after the fall, so the word came from real affection, not because Ajji was watching.

qa.q: How could Ajji help Ira understand titles?
qa.a: Keep correcting gently and, in moments like this, point out that anna is a word for someone older who looks after you.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya feel hearing 'Anna' whispered like that?
qa.a: Chaitanya would likely feel touched and trusted, hearing the title given freely.

grounding: Shows a child who repeats a title as a sound at first and later uses it with warmth for an older person who cares for her.

passage: In their Madrid flat, Clara, five, was learning new words from Mamá, who grew up in Pune. "Say Ines didi," Mamá said, pointing at Clara's big cousin. "Didi," Clara repeated, giggling at the sound. She called the baker "uncle" too, and the dog "didi". Ines laughed. Then one night Clara had a bad dream. She ran to Ines's bed. "Didi, can I stay?" Ines lifted the blanket. Clara snuggled in. "Didi means you look after me," she whispered.

qa.q: What did Clara call the dog?
qa.a: She called the dog "didi".

qa.q: How did Clara feel when she ran to Ines's bed?
qa.a: She felt scared after her bad dream and safe once Ines lifted the blanket.

qa.q: What helped Clara understand what "didi" means?
qa.a: Using the word every day and then being cared for by Ines at night showed her the word means warmth and looking after.

qa.q: How might Ines feel being called didi by Clara?
qa.a: Ines probably feels fond and protective, proud to be the big cousin Clara runs to.

grounding: It illustrates a child who copies a respect title first and later understands it carries warmth and rank.
